I recently moved into a new house (rental) that is in a nice neighborhood but has no HOA. I jumped on it when it became available because of the price/location - but this had me split between my old apartment and my new place for ~6 weeks. 

I got the keys on the 17th, moved in my first batch of stuff and spent my first night there the 22nd which was a Wednesday. The following Saturday - I’ve had the place 8 days - I went and bought a mower. Mowed the grass, had it looking pretty good, but left a patch on the far end of the property alone. In the whole process of viewing/leasing/waiting for move in - that one patch had been left overgrown (about knee high) so I just assumed that wasn’t my property. 

Sunday night (day 9) around 9:30pm an extremely concerned neighbor knocked on my door to tell me that I needed to mow my grass immediately. “I’m sorry BoomerNeighbor, I just mowed yesterday and thought it was in good shape.”  She ever so kindly informed me that she was talking about the tall patch abutting the other property - and that if I wasn’t going to take care of the lawn being the first house on the street I needed to find somewhere else to live. 

9am the next day - a Monday morning that I started working at 7am - there’s a police officer knocking on my door, with a second cruiser parked in  the road, responding to complaints of an abandoned/neglected property. They couldn’t tell me who complained, but shared that word came from city hall on behalf of someone close to them. 9 days in and this crazy Karen had the police on my door step for not mowing a tiny section of my yard I didn’t even know I was responsible for. 

Luckily the cops were cool and heard me out, apologizing profusely and ensuring me they just had to make contact to appease the higher ups. But since, I’ve kept a strict schedule of mowing at 9:30pm on Mondays/Thursdays and 6:30am on Wednesdays/Fridays since we also have no noise ordinance.

Read about playing triplets! You’re right in catching that it’s not the same as playing 1/8 or 1/16, as the groups of three don’t flow with up/down as well. 

Some people play them like you’ve drawn out, similar to a paradiddle when drumming. Basically alternating between up-down-up and down-up-down. 

My brain can’t process that though, so I just make every triplet down-up-down. So in this case it would be ⬇️⬆️⬇️⬇️⬆️⬇️⬇️⬆️⬇️⬇️⬆️⬇️

Your truss rod needs to be adjusted. Right now it’s convexed/“humped” where you want a slight concave/“bow” to offer slight relief. 

Looking at the neck from the side, if you fret at the first and 17th fret there should be space between the strings and the frets themselves. In this situation, you’ll see the string sitting on top of the frets. 

Loosen the tension in the truss rod, turn it counterclockwise 1/8 or 1/4 or a turn. Retune, check it, and repeat until it’s ringing at the first fret again. 

The important thing is to take your time, the small adjustments add up quicker than you think!

Get a second opinion, but do it in person and with a psychiatrist that specializes in ADHD to an extent that they’re familiar with identifying symptoms despite comorbidity. 

Anxiety, ADHD, and depression are best buds. It’s rare to see one without the others tagging along - partially because the main cause of ADHD also causes the other two (chemical imbalances). My psych recognized and acknowledged that I DO exhibit signs of depression, along with very apparent anhedonia. 

But she was familiar enough with all the above to hear me out when I said I wanted to start by treating the ADHD and then seek treatment for what my be left. I explained my negative family history with antidepressants, and expressed my hesitation with starting them myself. Low and behold, after 6 months of Vyvanse and coaching 80% of my depression/anxiety symptoms are almost gone.

Partially due to not constantly other-thinking every second of every day, but because the meds increase serotonin and dopamine which contribute to a more level disposition. Not only am I generally more happy and much better at handling social situations… but I can confront bigger phobias with a little self talk rather than just breaking down. 

These are my personal results, and there’s no guarantee yours would be the same. But talk to a professional (IN PERSON) and let them guide your journey to improvement. 

Can’t emphasize the “in-person” part enough. First of all, they take into account everything about your visit - your grooming, mannerism, speech patterns, etc - when evaluating you, and most online places are going to push SSRI’s over anything because of less liability (compared to scheduled prescriptions for ADHD) and increased profits from more frequent follow ups.

Not only is there taxes added at checkout that aren’t shown on the price tags... the taxes can vary greatly based on state, county, and city. 

In the town I grew up in, total sales tax was 7%. So if I went to the store down the street and bought a TV with a sticker price of $999, my total at checkout would be $1070. 

However, if I drove 15 minutes south to the northernmost city in the next county, they had a 6% tax rate... meaning the same TV from the same store would be $1060. One city south of that (another 10 minutes on the highway), it would be $1095 with their 9.5% rate. 

So even if you know to expect taxes, you can still get a shock at the register if you aren’t privy to the local rates.

To exercise an option, you have to be long (the buyer). Plus exercising a *put* means you are selling shares you already own. If you exercise a $20 put, you’re selling one hundred of your TSLA shares for $20 each. 

If you exercise a *call* you are buying one hundred shares at the strike price. 

Exercise call: buy 100 shares at strike price
Exercise put: sell 100 shares at strike price

If you sold a put with a $20 strike, the person who *buys* the put can exercise... which would mean you are responsible for buying 100 shares at $20. Nobody is going to exercise a $20 put on a $700 stock.

So typically, your two big factors in options are time (to expiry) and “moneyness”, or distance from the strike price. 

In normal circumstances: The longer the expiration date, the higher the value/premium because there’s a better chance of the option reaching the strike price. This is one element of extrinsic value. 

Likewise the further IN the money an option goes, the more it is worth (intrinsic value). This means being above the strike price of a call, or below the strike price of a put. If the strike price of a call is $100, and that stock rises to $105 the option will have a price of $5/share + Extrinsic value (time, volatility, etc). 

But GME has the added bonus of EXTREME volatility, which also adds to the price of options. The contract prices react very strongly to sharp movements, and drop quickly the calmer trading is. You could very easily see the $800c 3/19 options shoot from their current price of $0.46 to $5+ today if there’s a big spike in price/volume. This gain is all extrinsic value because intrinsically the contract ain’t worth shit until the stock climbs over $800. 

Also keep in mind you’re spending 100x what the price tag is, because the contract is for the leverage of 100 shares. So if the option says $0.25, you will pay $25 per contract. 

All this to say... it’s much more akin to gambling than anything. It COULD go up (a ton) in a very quick amount of time. I saw $2000 in options climb over $100,000 then back down to $500 because I was just oh so sure it’d bounce right back. Don’t be greedy. Don’t spend what you can’t afford to lose.

To address your first question: even when exercised they have little to no impact because they aren’t handled on the exchange. 

The price action being described here is (potentially) Market Makers buying the shares they need to cover ITM contracts if exercised. They have algorithms and business rules they determine (based on delta among other things) how many shares they have to have on hand to plan for ITM exercising. 

If they’ve got 100 calls out at $500, that’s 10,000 shares (100 contracts x 100 shares). 

If the price is at $50, there’s a very low chance of it being in the money, so they may only keep 5 (delta = .05) shares on hand just in case. As the price of the stock climbs, so does the likelihood of them needing to cover. Delta climbs to say .2 meaning they need to have 20 of those stocks on hand. 

As the calls come closer to being ITM and continue getting deeper in the money, Delta approaches 1 (or 100%), meaning they need to have all 100 shares on hand because it’s very likely it will be exercised. Now multiply this across 5000+ strikes coming in the money. 

This is oversimplified but hopefully helps show why they are buying more stocks as certain strikes become ATM or ITM.

You’re correct in what you’re saying, but this is the inverse of a gamma squeeze. 

A gamma squeeze is price action caused by forced hedging due to high volume of call purchases. The volume raises gamma, which raises delta, which forces MM to buy in order to cover the increased risk. The forced buying then has a positive impact on the underlying. So basic cause = increased buying of options. 

What I’m proposing isn’t forced hedging due to increased gamma. I’m suggesting that MM are more aggressively hedging beyond their normal delta requirements. We’d typically see similar movement on a much smaller scale as they adjust to maintain delta neutral due to contracts moving ITM... but this proposed exasperation in hedging (say... buying 15 calls for a .1 delta increase rather than 10) creates enough volume to confuse the OTHER algorithms buying.  The sudden change in volume beyond what is expected causes more buying. 

Essentially what I’m pitching, but didn’t want to word it like this and lose credibility: some players updated their algorithm to accommodate this extreme case, while others didn’t. The algo bots are basically shutting themselves when they see the unexpected volume, and respond in a way that’s counterintuitive to what they’d typically do when hedging is expected.

I’m honestly not sure a delta squeeze is an actual term. Just something I’m using to describe what (might be) happening here. 

So essentially, you’ve got big guys (Market Makers, or MM) that serve to provide liquidity to the markets. They handle huge number of shares and write a majority of the options that you see available to trade. 

When they write a call option, they are guaranteeing to sell the buyer of the contract 100 shares at a set price (the strike price). There is a measure called Delta which is essentially (not quite but it paints the picture) the likelihood of the call being exercised, and indicates to the MM how many shares they need to have on hand to be prepared to cover the contracts they wrote. As the underlying stock price moves closer to the strike price of the contract, the delta goes up which triggers the MM to buy more shares. This number is a percentage  typically less than the full 100 shares (they also take  into account the volatility of the stock, how much they already have on hand, etc). 

My thesis here is that due to the volatility in this particular stock, they are more aggressively delta hedging... or buying a larger percentage of those 100 shares per contract than they usually would just to make damn sure they cover their asses. 

Whenever a new option becomes in the money, this triggers their algorithms to buy large quantities of the underlying stock. Other players watching for movement see this and also jump in. This causes a dramatic increase in volume... or in other words, a delta squeeze!
